27890.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse jórtra (“to ruminate”), also jórta (“to ruminate”). The Old Norse verb continues a prehistoric Germanic formation containing Proto-Germanic *idi- (“again, anew; back”) and an otherwise unattested Germanic verbal base conventionally reconstructed as *rukijan- (“to belch, regurgitate”), ultimately related to Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewg- (“to belch, roar”).
Compare Norwegian Nynorsk jorta and jorte, Faroese jótra, Icelandic jórtra and Swedish jorta (“to ruminate, chew the cud”) (dialectal, obsolete).

1004274.etyen:
From lørdag (“Saturday”) + pizza (“pizza”), with linking -s- (“interfix”), literally “Saturday pizza”, referring to pizza eaten as a regular Saturday-evening meal. The first element, lørdag, is inherited from Danish lørdag, from Old Danish løghærdagh, ultimately from Old Norse laugardagr (“bath day; Saturday”). The second element, pizza, is borrowed from Italian pizza. The compound is first attested in 2003.
The term predates the product name Grandiosa Lørdagspizza, introduced in 2006.
Compare the equivalent Swedish formation lördagspizza (“Saturday pizza”).

1004786.etyen: Inherited from Old Norse Brattsberg. The second element is berg (“rock, cliff, hill”), while the first is related to brattr (“steep”). The exact formation and the medial -s- are uncertain. The name has traditionally been interpreted as literally “the steep rock” or “the steep cliff”; other proposals analyse the first element as a lost topographical name or as a neuter noun meaning “something steep; a cliff face”. The surname is habitational, derived from one of the places named Bratsberg.

1005042.etyen:
A fixed phrase consisting of the imperative ha (“to have”), the pronoun det (“it”) and adverbial godt (“well”), literally “have it well”. As a farewell, the phrase expresses a wish for the addressee's continued well-being. The shortened farewell ha det (“goodbye, bye”) is an ellipsis of this expression or ha det bra (“goodbye, take care”).
Compare the parallel formations Norwegian Nynorsk ha det godt, Danish hav det godt and Swedish ha det gott (“goodbye, take care”).
